Vision & Values
Our founders, Mr Poularas and Mr Speed, opened their first school in 1967 with a bold ambition to create a genuinely caring and engaged community with a strong sense of its role in the lives of the local and global families it served.
From those early beginnings, the core principles of community, positive change, excellence, and internationalism continue to guide ACS today.
An ACS education has at its heart the idea of readiness: when they leave ACS, our students face the world as effective, confident, and caring individuals who are ready to act, lead, care, and change the world.
At the highest level, our purpose is to inspire the world’s next global thinkers and doers. As we look to the future, ACS remains as true to its international education roots now as ever.
Our charitable mission
ACS Hillingdon is part of the ACS International Schools group, a dynamic, people-focused charity that advances education. ACS International Schools became a registered UK charity in 2018.
As a charity, ACS is committed to advancing education by providing a range of means-tested bursary places and working locally and internationally in collaboration with schools and communities to share expertise and resources to enrich the education of our partner communities and ourselves.
Our Core Values
ACS has five core values and is committed to living and working by these to ensure we achieve the aims and ambitions we hold for ourselves and our students.

When we chose ACS Hillingdon School four years ago, we were drawn by its excellent infrastructure, welcoming atmosphere, supportive admissions team, and its truly international community. We hoped it would be a place where our child would not only excel academically but also grow into a confident, compassionate and globally minded individual. Looking back, we can say with complete confidence that it was one of the best decisions we have made. If given the choice again, we would wholeheartedly choose this school. Exceptional teachers, outstanding university counsellors, enriching extracurricular opportunities, and a genuinely inclusive culture have made these four years transformative. The school's commitment to inquiry, international-mindedness, and holistic development has prepared our child not just for university, but for life.

THE ENVIRONMENT WE CREATE IS PERSONAL AND POSITIVE – DESIGNED TO STIMULATE CURIOSITY AND A LOVE OF KNOWLEDGE.
In Upper School, our focus is on inspiring our students to think for themselves, work hard, and make creative connections between ideas to arrive at a deeper understanding of the world and their place in it. We don’t ‘teach to the test’, although our examination results are excellent. Instead, we personalise our teaching to enable students to reach their own conclusions, set challenging personal goals and to have a positive impact on their local, national, and international community.

Grades 5-8
Students in Grades 5-8 embark on an exciting educational journey that blends a flexible, enquiry-based approach with rigorous academics. Our curriculum uses internationally recognised standards and is designed to cater to the diverse needs of our student body.
During these formative years, students are encouraged to explore a wide array of subjects, allowing them to develop critical thinking skills, creativity, and a lifelong love of learning. In addition to our robust academic programme, we offer excellent co-curricular opportunities. Students can participate in a variety of arts, sports, clubs, and activities, ensuring a well-rounded education that nurtures both their academic and personal growth.
During these years, every ACS student is inspired to achieve their full potential in a supportive and dynamic environment.
Grades 9-10
Building on the strong foundation laid in Grades 5-8, our Grades 9-10 programme continues to offer a rigorous and flexible curriculum tailored to our diverse student body. These years are designed to provide greater student agency and autonomy, allowing students to take charge of their educational journey.
Our comprehensive curriculum is complemented by a plethora of co-curricular opportunities. Students can engage in leadership roles, participate in overseas trips, and lead from the front, whether within clubs and activities, student organisations, or curriculum-based roles. These experiences help our students develop into well-rounded individuals and global citizens.
Our students in Grades 9-10 are empowered to reach their full potential, both academically and personally, in a vibrant and supportive environment.
Grades 11-12
In Grades 11 and 12, we proudly offer a variety of globally recognised programmes, including the IB Diploma Programme (IBDP), IB Career-related Programme (IBCP), Advanced Placement (AP), and High School Diploma (HS). This range of options ensures that every student can find a path that suits their interests and academic goals.
Our expert University and Careers Counselling team supports students with their course selection and applications for further education. Each year, ACS Hillingdon students move on to attend some of the best institutions across the globe. We are extremely proud of our ACS Hillingdon graduates, who leave us equipped with the skills to make an impact on the global stage.
Hear from one of our graduating students
In ACS’s University Admissions Officers’ research conducted over the last ten years, the IB and AP programmes have been shown to significantly outperform A-levels in developing qualities such as a global outlook, open-mindedness, self-management, coping under pressure and analytical thinking.
Our curriculum
Our broad and flexible curriculum enables students to learn what they love. Students can select from a wide range of pathways that can be tailored to their individual strengths and aspirations. We also offer various opportunities for students to find and follow their individual strengths, including an impressive range of co-curricular activities, clubs, field trips, and volunteering opportunities.
Students learn to think independently, cultivate their talents, and take ownership of their learning journey. This prepares them to graduate as confident individuals, caring contributors, and effective learners ready to make a global impact.

Community & Culture at ACS Hillingdon
What makes ACS Hillingdon distinctive is its warm, welcoming atmosphere – a place where the vibrancy of London meets a close-knit school community. Despite our location in one of the world’s most dynamic cities, the school maintains a nurturing, family feel that sets it apart from other private schools in London. With smaller class sizes and a supportive environment, every student is known, valued, and encouraged to thrive.
Our dedicated teachers, pastoral leaders, and university counsellors work in partnership with families to guide each learner’s journey and ensure they reach their personal best. Frequently Asked Questions about ACS Hillingdon
Does ACS Hillingdon International School require entrance exams for admission?
No, ACS Hillingdon International School is broadly-selective and does not require entrance exams. Admissions decisions are made holistically by assessing previous school reports, teacher references, standardised test scores, and student questionnaires.
Does ACS Hillingdon offer mid-year or rolling admissions?
Yes, ACS Hillingdon operates a rolling admissions policy year-round. Relocating international families and local transfer students can apply and enrol at any point during the academic year, subject to grade-level availability.
What age range does ACS Hillingdon International School educate?
ACS Hillingdon educates co-educational day students aged 3 to 18 years old (Pre-Kindergarten through Grade 12 / UK Year 13). The school is divided into Lower School (Ages 3–10), Middle School (Ages 10–14), and High School (Ages 14–18).
What High School qualifications are available at ACS Hillingdon?
High School students aged 16 to 18 (Grades 11–12) at ACS Hillingdon can pursue the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IBDP), the IB Career-related Programme (IBCP), American Advanced Placement (AP) courses, the Global Citizenship Diploma or a NEASC-accredited US High School Diploma.
Does ACS Hillingdon teach the British National Curriculum (GCSEs or A-Levels)?
No, ACS Hillingdon International School does not offer GCSEs or A-Levels. Instead, it provides internationally recognised qualification pathways based on the International Baccalaureate (IB) and American Advanced Placement (AP) curricula.
Where is ACS Hillingdon International School located?
ACS Hillingdon International School is situated on an 11-acre estate featuring a Grade II listed historic mansion house on Vine Lane, Hillingdon, Greater London (UB10 0BE), approximately 14 miles west of Central London.

Tanisi Garg balanced founding a student newspaper, captaining the volleyball team and running a school society’s finances alongside one of the most demanding qualifications on offer. She scored 43 out of 45 in the International Baccalaureate – the equivalent of around five A* grades – and is off to the London School of Economics. Rudra Mathur made the brave decision to study four higher level subjects over the required three and achieved a score less than one percent globally get – 45 out of 45 and is also off to the London School of Economics.
Tanisi Garg has spent her sixth form doing rather more than her exams. Alongside the International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma Programme (DP), she helped found The Hawk Eye, the school’s student newspaper, as its Creative Head, captained the volleyball team and served as treasurer of the National Honour Society, a US honour society that selects members on academic record, service, leadership and character. She scored 43 points out of 45 – the equivalent of around five A* grades at A-level – and will read Accounting and Finance at the London School of Economics.
Tanisi said: “I chose the IB because I wanted something challenging that would prepare me for university, and I liked that I didn’t have to narrow my studies too early. Balancing The Hawk Eye, volleyball and the National Honour Society with the demands of the IB wasn’t always easy, but it taught me to plan ahead, prioritise and ask for help when I needed it. Looking back, those experiences made me much more resilient.”
For Tanisi, the IB offered the academic challenge she was looking for while allowing her to develop interests and skills beyond the classroom.
Rudra Mathur took the unusual and demanding step of sitting four Higher Level subjects rather than the usual three. He was not sure what he wanted to specialise in at sixteen, and the breadth of the IB meant he did not have to decide too soon. He will now read Politics and Economics at the London School of Economics.
Rudra said: “If I went back to do it [IB] again, I would once again choose four Higher Levels. It meant I got depth in everything I cared about instead of having to pick a lane at sixteen. It challenged me in a positive way, greatly improved my time management and prepared me to prioritise and manage heavy workloads.”
Rudra’s achievements at ACS Hillingdon have extended well beyond his academic results. He has served as President of the National Honour Society, chaired and won accolades at Model United Nations conferences, and was selected as one of 400 students globally to serve as a student advocate for a leading financial daily. He has also conducted research with Harvard professors through the Cambridge Centre for International Research (CCIR) programme and taken leading roles in the school’s musicals.
Together, Tanisi and Rudra illustrate two very different approaches to the transition from school to university: one student with a clear academic and career direction, and another who deliberately chose breadth and exploration before deciding where his interests would take him.
Their results form part of a strong year for the IB Diploma at ACS Hillingdon. Almost every Hillingdon student who sat the IB Diploma this summer gained the full Diploma, a pass rate of 97 per cent. The year group averaged 37 points, against a world average of 30 – the equivalent of three A* at A-level on the school’s comparison scale. The school’s highest score was 45 out of 45, a perfect score achieved by fewer than one per cent of students worldwide.
Not every Hillingdon student takes the full Diploma. The school also offers the IB Career-related Programme, which pairs a career focus with two or three of the Diploma’s Higher Level subjects. Every student on the programme passed this year and all achieved at least a 5 out of 7 in each of their Higher Level subjects.
Hillingdon also offers the Advanced Placement (AP) programme, which lets a student specialise rather than spread across six subjects. This year 22 Hillingdon students sat AP exams, scoring an average of 3.6 out of 5, and more than 91% scored 3 or above, well above the world average for these rigorous, University-level courses.
The ‘Class of 2026’ are heading to UK universities including Imperial College London, King’s College London, LSE, Bath, Exeter and St Andrews. Others are going further afield – McGill in Canada, the University of Melbourne in Australia, ESCP Business School in France, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Bocconi in Italy, IE University in Spain, and, in the United States, Babson College, Boston University and the University of Arizona.
Martin Hall, Head of School at ACS Hillingdon, said the results should make people think harder about how schools are judged.
He explained that: “There is a national habit of measuring a school by its A-level grades alone.
But the people who pick university students are looking for something broader. In a survey of 65 admissions officers we published this year, a large majority said the IB Diploma – not A-levels – is the best preparation to thrive at university, and they now rate what a student knows as being no more important than what they can do with it. Both students are case in point. They have run their own initiatives, led teams and managed their time, and they have the grades too. That is what universities tell us they now depend on, and we do it without selecting a single child on ability.”
That survey, the University Admissions Officers Report 2026, was carried out for ACS International Schools with the IB Schools and Colleges Association. It found the IB Diploma rated 23 per cent higher than A-levels across the skills universities say they now want most, including independent research and the ability to manage competing deadlines.
I chose the IB because I wanted something challenging that would prepare me for university, and I liked that I didn’t have to narrow my studies too early. Balancing The Hawk Eye, volleyball and the National Honour Society with the demands of the IB wasn’t always easy, but it taught me to plan ahead, prioritise and ask for help when I needed it. Looking back, those experiences made me much more resilient.

English as an Additional Language (EAL)
At ACS Hillingdon, we believe that achieving proficiency in academic English is more than just overcoming a challenge—it’s about celebrating the advantages of being multilingual.
Our English as an Additional Language (EAL) programme helps students develop the fluency in English they need to thrive in a global community and succeed in International Baccalaureate Diploma and Career-related Programmes as well as rigorous US College Board Advanced Placement courses.
The EAL Programme
The EAL programme is personalised to each English language learner.
Intensive English Courses
Focused, small-group lessons designed to rapidly build foundational English skills, vocabulary, and grammatical accuracy. Students have lessons led by an EAL specialist teacher to attain proficient levels of listening, reading, speaking, and writing.
Critical Academic Language Proficiency
Specialist teachers provide in-class support for courses across all academic subject areas. Students learn how to analyse complex texts, participate in academic discussions, write sophisticated essays, and understand nuanced instructions crucial for success in advanced courses.
Monitoring Student Progress
Each EAL learner is supported by a case manager who closely monitors their development of Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills along with more formal academic English.
Language is central to all aspects of our lives, both personal and professional. EAL students learn how to engage flexibly with different linguistic and cultural groups, increasing their competence in productive, receptive, and interactive English language skills.
In-class Support (UDL)
Our EAL specialists collaborate with classroom teachers, using the Universal Design for Learning (UDL) framework to ensure that EAL students can access information and demonstrate their learning. Students continue to improve grammar and accuracy, vocabulary and pronunciation, and organisation. They develop sophisticated understanding of meaning, purpose, audience, register, and structure of English texts.
Learning Beyond the Classroom

Who is the EAL Programme For?
The EAL programme is designed for motivated students joining ACS Hillingdon who have a broad range of English language proficiency. It is available to qualified students who are ready to engage in academic and co-curricular activities, contribute to our multilingual community, and succeed in rigorous academic courses, including an opportunity to earn the prestigious IB Bilingual Diploma.

IB Career-related Programme (IBCP)
At ACS Hillingdon, the IBCP is a flagship programme shaped by experience, academic rigour, and a clear understanding of where modern education is heading. Among London schools, our depth of expertise enables us to deliver one of the most well developed and intentionally designed IBCP experiences available to students today.
The International Baccalaureate Career-related Programme (IBCP) is a modern qualification that prepares students for their chosen careers while completing an IB Diploma recognised worldwide by universities and employers.
IBCP students are equipped for the future world of work, where transferable skills and learning attitudes are increasingly crucial for success. They benefit from workshops led by industry experts in fields such as film and performing arts, alongside a rigorous and balanced IB programme that offers flexibility with a wide range of IBDP subjects.
As a group of schools, we have been teaching the IB for over fifty years, including a comprehensive suite of IB Art options encompassing visual, performing arts, and film. Our expertise in these areas has enabled us to pioneer the adoption of the IBCP, offering a unique programme in Theatre Arts and Digital Arts (games design, animation, and visual effects).
The Programme Framework
Specifically designed to empower students who want to specialise in, and focus on, a career-related education, the programme’s three-part framework comprises:
*It is recommended that students also take maths, if not IBDP, at High School level.
Two-four IB Diploma Programme courses*
Language development portfolio
How does the IBCP prepare students?
Personal and Professional Skills
Preparing students for future leadership roles in their industry is a crucial aspect of the IBCP. Students are equipped with tools highly sought after by employers, such as project management skills, effective written and verbal communication, and proficiency in navigating business environments, including current industry protocols. They are supported by visits to professional environments like Pinewood Studios.
Reflective Project
Students explore various global perspectives on an issue affecting their chosen industry. They apply research, critical thinking, and evaluation skills to assess the ethical problem and its potential impact on workers, consumers, employers, and other stakeholders.
Service Learning
Helping others is central to the IBCP, and students participate in several service projects, including at least one designed and implemented within the local community. This involves a range of volunteering opportunities both within the school and with our local partner organisations, allowing students to make a positive impact while gaining insights from diverse perspectives.
I was able to choose classes that would better prepare me for university and continue my passion, while still receiving a well-rounded education. Knowing I wanted to study arts at university, the IBCP was the perfect fit for me.
Theatre Arts
IBCP Theatre Arts is a course tailored for students with an interest and passion for performing arts, directing, and production.
This unique course focuses on devising and analysing theatre, developing various acting styles and skills ranging from classical to contemporary texts, and directing for stage and set design.
Each student will build their own portfolio, which becomes part of their application for related courses at university.
Digital Arts
ACS Hillingdon has been a longstanding partner of the UK film industry, maintaining strong ties with Pinewood Studios, known for Hollywood blockbusters like the James Bond, Star Wars, and Jurassic Park franchises.
The course encompasses animation, 3D modelling, game design, visual effects, and computer programming, culminating in the development of a personal portfolio.
Students will gain from collaboration with industry specialists and mentors throughout the two-year course.
Understanding the IBCP
Why choose the IBCP?
How is the IBCP assessed?
Why choose the IBCP?
The IBCP offers a flexible approach to the International Baccalaureate, allowing students to select courses aligned with their chosen career or area of study. It enables them to explore the practical application of their studies, whether in drama and performing arts, technical careers in production for film and theatre, or digital arts industries like games design, animation, and VFX.
In an ever-changing job market, skills valued by employers—such as creativity and problem-solving—are at the core of the IBCP curriculum. Students receive professional guidance and support, including participating in workshops led by industry professionals.
Rooted in the values and principles of the International Baccalaureate, the IBCP encourages students to study a language of their choice and consider global perspectives. They examine challenges facing their chosen industry and apply ethical theory to evaluate these issues. The course aims to develop not only industry-relevant knowledge, skills, and attitudes but also provides a broader perspective to equip students as future leaders in their fields.
How does the IBCP differ from the IBDP?
In the IBDP, students are required to study six courses to enable them to gain a more well-rounded qualification ahead of starting university and entering the workplace. This offers them the opportunity to explore what they are passionate about before they select a specific subject for university.
In the IBCP, students can select up to 4 subjects from any DP subject area, which might include studying multiple arts subjects, for example. While it is always recommended that for university requirements, students undertake some maths and some English, we offer High School diploma level non-IB courses in English and maths for those students who wish to align their IB subject choices to their preferred area, freeing them up to choose what best suits their passions, interests, and aspirations.
How is the IBCP assessed?
The IB Careers Programme (IBCP) follows the same programme as the IBDP for the 2-4 IBDP subjects, with students attending the same lessons and gaining the same qualification.
In addition to these subjects, students gain an external qualification for theatre arts, or games design, animation and VFX, which are recognised by universities as excellent entry points that allow students to build a portfolio that makes them stand out from the crowd when applying to courses in these careers.
In addition, to be awarded the IBCP diploma, students need only to fulfill the core requirements that relate to the IB approach and philosophy. A reflective project of 3000 words, a portfolio of language development and a reflective log of service and volunteering opportunities, similar to the IBDP core, enables them to achieve the IBCP diploma.
Is the IBCP accepted by universities and colleges around the world?
The IB is widely accepted by top universities around the world. What sets students apart in the IBCP is that their career related study gives them a professional portfolio and a range of experiences in industry that will stand out in their college applications and personal statements. The industry-orientated, creative approach to building a portfolio with a range of skills is recognised by universities as a strong indicator of a student who is prepared to extend their own learning, in a similar way to their own university level courses.
Hear from our IBCP students
From an admissions perspective, this looks like a very exciting development. These programmes are good feeders for universities like ours. And it is obviously always good to receive applications from students already engaged in the subject area.

University and Careers Counselling
Well-rounded global citizens
At ACS Hillingdon, we take great pride in developing effective, confident, and caring individuals who leave ACS as well-rounded global citizens ready to act, lead, and change the world.
Our University and Careers Counsellors work with each student individually to offer bespoke, student-centred, and expert provision to meet a student’s needs by valuing their individual strengths.
From Grade 10 (aged 15/16) onwards, students begin to explore opportunities, are advised on subject selection, and are guided through the application process by their nominated Counsellor.
The Counsellors maximise student opportunities by providing comprehensive, honest information that allows students and families to make informed decisions and find the “best fit” university or pathway. The Counsellors define “fit” as meeting the academic, emotional, geographical, and financial needs of the student.
Counsellors support students in the following ways
Our Counsellors have a wealth of experience working with a breadth of universities and colleges around the world navigating challenging admission requirements and advocating for students. Each year students attend world-class universities and colleges around the world, with the majority attending higher education institutions in the UK and the US.
Career research

Organising University and College visits and fairs
The key benefits of our University and Careers Counselling provision
Each year, our students apply to a whole range of countries: the UK, US, Canada, Netherlands, Japan, Italy, France, Spain, and more. This keeps our knowledge and expertise in global study destinations up to date, and we are connected to a network of admissions officers across the world.
We have a broad understanding of different qualifications and educational experiences. Some of our students take a mix of High School, IB, and AP courses across grades 9-12 (years 10-13), and some may join ACS at different entry points with different qualifications, subject options, and understanding of university requirements.
We have extensive experience navigating challenging admission requirements for different degree courses across the world. We advise students carefully on subject selection to ensure academic goals are in line with future aspirations and that students take subjects they will enjoy and succeed in.
All of our staff have experienced living or studying in countries around the world, and we draw upon those experiences when talking and working with students. We deeply empathise with students who may have moved from, or are moving to, their third, fourth, or fifth country, and understand how to support these transitions.

The Class of 2024 at ACS Hillingdon received offers from 149 different universities across 8 countries
Our University and Careers Counsellors have lived in 9 different countries combined
Our students choose to pursue a range of pathways after school, including university, apprenticeships, performing arts conservatories, and military service
We advocate for our students with university admission officers by attending global university events and conferences

University & College Counselling FAQs
Which universities do ACS students go to?
Each year, ACS Hillingdon students apply to an impressive array of global destinations, including universities in the UK, the US, the Netherlands, Canada, France, Japan, Italy, Spain, and more. They are admitted to study at selective universities, including UK Russell Group and US Ivy League schools.
Our students also go on to study in a wide range of specialist courses and best-in-class academic programmes– many in unique destinations and with a distinct international flair. This diverse range of applications reflects the individual interests of our students and the global nature of their aspirations.
How early does university counselling begin?
We offer a personalised, student-centred approach to university preparation, starting with career education and academic pathway guidance throughout their ACS education. The counsellors feed into subject selection processes for students in Grades 8 and 9. In addition, they lead parent information meetings focused on identifying best-fit post-graduation pathways for students.
By grade 10 (ages 15-16), they are making important choices about course selection for university. In grade 11, through one-on-one sessions, we guide students to explore their academic and career interests, ensuring they are making informed decisions about their future.
Do you help with UCAS/Common App applications?
Yes. We work closely with students to prepare the individual components of the application process, such as personal statements, interviews, and extracurricular activities specific to each university destination. This includes creating and completing Common App and UCAS accounts. These components are critical for distinguishing a student’s application, and our team helps students develop a compelling applicant profile. Our students present themselves as well-rounded individuals, ready to illustrates their readiness to contribute to the university community and beyond.
Do you support applications outside the UK/US?
Our Counsellors are highly experienced in navigating the often-complex admissions requirements of universities around the world and use their expertise to advocate for each student. We also maintain strong connections with a wide network of admissions officers, giving our students an added advantage when applying to competitive institutions. We’ve invited global universities to explain application processes in different countries, hosted international university fairs, organised external speakers through the Scholars Programme, and shared additional external opportunities on our Weekly Universities and Careers Corner.
Is the counselling personalised to each student’s interests and goals?
At ACS Hillingdon, we believe that the path to university should not only be about academic achievement but also about finding the right environment where students can thrive, both intellectually and personally.
Our goal is to help students become confident, caring, effective people who are ready to act, lead, and change the world. Central to this mission is the process of identifying “best-fit” universities and other post-graduation learning opportunities. We are proud of how our University and College Counselling team works to support each student through this pivotal stage in their academic journey.
How do you support students who are unsure about their next steps?
We encourage students to engage in experiential opportunities like taster courses, open days, and work experiences to explore interests, guide them in reflecting on their skills and strengths, and invite guest speakers from universities and industry to share insights and inspire informed choices.
We also make families aware of the implications of subject and programme choices for university and career pathways, to support informed decision making that aligns with students’ goals and future opportunities.
What about guidance for apprenticeships or non-traditional routes? Do you support students interested in gap years or internships?
We invite current apprentices to speak at Careers Day, giving students firsthand insights into non-university pathways. We also work with careers organisations like Springpod to demystify apprenticeship pathways. Additionally, we encourage all students to develop employability skills, drafting CVs, researching careers and industries so that, regardless of the pathway they choose, they are well-prepared for the world of work.
For students considering gap years, we help students map out potential opportunities including travel, study, volunteer work, work experience, and language development.
Can students apply to multiple countries at the same time?
We encourage students to think about the time required to prepare strong applications and to think ahead to organise their time. Students can apply to multiple destinations simultaneously, but we advise them to be pragmatic with their applications to manage their workload and mental health.
Are references and transcripts provided by the school?
Yes, the counsellors manage academic documents for various destinations. This includes transcript and predicted grades, letter preparation, enrolment verifications, and letter of recommendation management.
How are parents kept informed about the university planning process?
We believe that students’ university journeys are a team effort, and we work to keep parents informed about admissions trends and opportunities for students. We host parent information meetings (PIMs) on university and career topics, ranging from what an Oxbridge university experience is like to financial aid opportunities at North American universities. Additionally, we lead sessions at Open House and invite parents to be a part of the subject selection processes.
Can parents book meetings with the college counsellors?
We encourage all parents to attend our PIMs and Open House sessions to learn about opportunities for their children and how to best support them. We meet with all Grade 10 families during the subject selection process and welcome communication from Grade 11 and 12 families concerning university applications or career plans.
Do UK universities accept IB and AP qualifications instead of standard GCSEs and A-Levels?
Yes. Most UK universities accept a range of internationally recognised qualifications alongside GCSEs and A-Levels, including the International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma, Advanced Placement (AP), the European Baccalaureate, and other national qualifications. Entry requirements vary by university and course, but these alternative pathways are widely recognised for undergraduate admissions.

“Leaders’ vision and values inform all aspects of the school’s work and support an environment which promotes pupils’ wellbeing effectively.”

“Effective self-evaluation is used to translate the school’s aims and ethos into actions which have pupils’ wellbeing and achievement as their focus.”
“Pastoral leadership across the school, including in early years, is highly effective.”
2. Quality of education, training and recreation
“Pupils enjoy their learning. They typically experience lessons where teachers’ subject knowledge, skills and enthusiasm enable all groups of pupils to achieve success and find the work interesting.”
“The school’s democratic ethos and strategic work on encouraging pupils to voice their perspectives has resulted in pupils who are confident and sophisticated in their verbal exchanges with adults and each other, who contribute freely to class discussion and are prepared to take risks in their learning.”
“Pupils across the school experience a broad and creative curriculum which is appropriate to their abilities and needs and which covers all the required subject disciplines.”
“Pupils’ achievement and participation in creative and performing arts courses is high.”
“The extensive extra-curricular programme allows for a wide range of interests to be stimulated and nurtured.”
3. Pupils’ physical and mental health and emotional wellbeing
“Pupils’ emotional wellbeing is very well supported by the systems leaders have put in place to track any pastoral matters and ensure that staff supporting the pupils are well informed about their pastoral needs.”
“Behaviour is good, bullying rare and pupils are confident that systems exist to deal fairly with issues should they arise.”
“Leaders shape an ethos of mutual respect where pupils appreciate the individuality of others.”
“Counselling services within the school provide pupils with emotional support should they need it.”
“Children in the early years learn how to live healthily, for example by cooking simple dishes in a specialist kitchen in their building or by growing vegetables in the school allotment.”
4. Pupils’ social and economic education and contribution to society
“Pupils proceed to universities and employment across the world, benefitting from effective, balanced and personalised careers advice that prepares them effectively for their next steps. Leaders give mindful attention to transition points within the school so that pupils are confident in progressing to the next stage of their education”
“The school enables pupils to develop their sense of responsibility to those around them and the wider world.”
“Leaders utilise the school’s international curriculum to promote a global outlook and appreciation of diversity and respect for fundamental British values such as mutual respect and individual freedom.”
“Leaders provide multiple opportunities for pupils from a young age to experience responsibility and leadership.”
“Belonging and kindness are key values and are encouraged through the taught curriculum, policies, the topics of assemblies and the PSHE programme.”
“Pupils actively engage with the local community through, for example, creating workshops on nutrition for pupils at a partner primary school, organising a clothing and toy donation drive for re-homed refugee families and supporting the organisation of a science and technology day at an amusement park.”

“Safeguarding is a whole school priority.”
“Governors and leaders monitor the school’s safeguarding arrangements regularly to ensure their sustained effectiveness.”
“Staff are well trained and understand what actions to take if concerns arise.”
“Pupils feel safe in school and secure about how to report worries about themselves or others.”
“Pupils across the school experience a broad and creative curriculum which is appropriate to their abilities and needs and which covers all the required subject disciplines.”

Home Language Enrichment
Programme Overview
The free Home Language Enrichment (HLE) Programme at ACS Hillingdon is dedicated to helping organise language classes for students’ home language.
This programme is designed to help students in Grades 1 to 10 whose first language isn’t English, to maintain their home language and culture.
We recognise the importance of multilingualism and how children who maintain their mother tongue, preserve their indigenous culture through language.
The lessons are offered once a week for forty minutes after school. Students will engage in language and cultural activities designed to enrich their appreciation and use of their respective languages.
Students will read, write, and converse in the target language, and wherever possible, high-interest materials (books, magazines, websites) from their home country will be used.
The classes are an excellent opportunity for multilingual children to unite with others from their language backgrounds. As an example, in recent years, we have offered classes in Italian, Danish, Spanish, German, French, Russian, Arabic, Chinese, Swedish, Japanese, Turkish, Urdu, Hindi.
To speak another language is to have one more window from which to look at the world.

English as an Additional Language (EAL)
At ACS Hillingdon, the Lower School’s English as an Additional Language (EAL) programme supports young learners in a welcoming environment in which they can make friends and engage with the school’s curriculum—preparing them for success.
English Language Learners in Early Years
Early and primary years students learn English in a supportive immersion setting, in which they use their full linguistic repertoire (all languages they know) to learn and communicate. We recognise that multilingual students think and express themselves in a fluid way, using their different languages as one interconnected system.
This ‘translanguaging’ promotes a more inclusive and engaging learning environment in which students speak, belong, and thrive as they learn English together.
Specialist EAL Teaching
We recognise the unique strengths that EAL learners bring, including their cultural and personal experiences, and we use these assets to create a positive and supportive learning environment.
Our dedicated EAL specialists work closely with Lower School students across a range of English language competencies, providing personalised support to help build confidence and meet essential content learning goals. Each student’s progress is carefully monitored to ensure they receive the appropriate guidance.
